questions.stem: A 60-year-old woman presented with progressive ataxia and dizziness. She gave a clear history of a flu-like illness and distinctive rash following a tick bite several years earlier in Slovenia. A lumbar puncture was performed and showed a lymphocytic pleocytosis, raised protein, and oligoclonal bands. MRI imaging showed no lesions.
questions.lead_in: What is the most likely causative organism?

options.text: Babesia microti
Borrelia afzelii
Borrelia garinii
Tickborne encephalitis virus
Treponema pallidum

questions.explanation: Borrelia garinii Borrelia afzelii and Borrelia garinii are both part of the Borrelia burgdorferi sensu lato group. B. afzelii is found in Europe and is associated with acrodermatitis chronica atrophicans whereas B. garinii , which is also found in Europe, is associated with neurologic presentations of Lyme disease. Babesiosis is also a tickborne disease. It is a parasitic infection affecting red blood cells, but neurologic disease is not described. Tickborne encephalitis virus is a member of the family Flaviviridae. It is a viral infection with acute onset of symptoms (incubation 7–14 days), and rash is not described. Treponema pallidum may cause neurosyphilis with an aseptic meningitis, but the rash is not typical for syphilis, nor would a tick bite be related.
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 2 Q22

questions.stem: A 25-year-old woman presented with a new skin lesion. She was hiking in Provincetown, MA earlier during the week though she did not remember any tick bites. She was usually well and was only taking the oral contraceptive pill. She had no known drug allergies.
questions.lead_in: What is the most appropriate action?

options.text: Acute and convalescent serologies for Borrelia burgdorferi
Borrelia burgdorferi PCR testing
ELISA and Western blot for Borrelia burgdorferi
Start 14 days doxycycline
Take a skin biopsy

questions.explanation: Start 14 days doxycycline Early Lyme with erythema migrans or disseminated erythema migrans is a clinical diagnosis. Serologies may be falsely negative in early infections. Serology is only sent for atypical or difficult cases. Lyme clinical diagnosis Early localized Confirmatory ELISA and western blot Early disseminated Late stage Doxycycline or amoxicillin for 14-21 days Meningitis or heart block: Ceftriaxone x 28 days Doxycycline or amoxicillin for 28 days CNS complications: Ceftriaxone x 28 days Doxycycline or amoxicillin for 14-21 days
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 5 Q32

questions.stem: A 23-year-old woman presented with a 3-day history of an enlarging skin lesion and mild myalgia. She reported that she had removed an engorged tick 2 weeks previously after walking in the New Forest, UK. On examination: Neurologic examination was normal.
questions.lead_in: What is the most appropriate action?

options.text: Hold antibiotics pending serology results
Reassure that this is a tick bite reaction only
Start ceftriaxone 2 g OD for 14–21 days
Start ciprofloxacin 500 mg BD for 14–21 days
Start doxycycline 100 mg BD for 14–21 days

questions.explanation: Start doxycycline 100 mg BD for 14–21 days The lesion shown is erythema migrans and is typical for early Lyme disease. It is a clinical diagnosis and serology may initially be negative. Guidelines state that treatment with doxycycline should be given for 14–21 days. (Image from Nadelman RB. Erythema migrans. Infect Dis Clin North Am. 2015;29(2):211–239.)
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 6 Q14

questions.stem: A 51-year-old woman was admitted with a 2-day history of dizziness. She had been out gardening all summer. She initially thought the dry heat was making her dehydrated, but her symptoms persisted despite water intake. She was a college professor in Connecticut and gardened every afternoon. She had not noted any tick bites or rashes. She had a history of osteoarthritis of her knees, hypertension, and raised cholesterol. She took occasional acetaminophen (paracetamol) and was taking amlodipine and atorvastatin. Physical exam was unremarkable except for a heart rate of 47 beats/minute. ECG: Initial enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay and a confirmatory Western blot assay were positive for Borrelia burgdorferi.
questions.lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial treatment?

options.text: Amoxicillin
Ceftriaxone
Cefuroxime
Doxycycline
Pacemaker placement

questions.explanation: Ceftriaxone The patient has AV block from Lyme disease. Treatment of Lyme disease depends on stage and severity. For heart block which requires hospitalization, parenteral ceftriaxone is the initial treatment of choice. Doxycycline may be used to complete the course, or for a full course of treatment in ambulatory patients with cardiac Lyme disease.
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 7 Q15

questions.stem: A 35-year-old man presented with a markedly swollen right knee. It was not particularly painful but examination showed a massive effusion. Two months earlier he had a rash on his back which he thought was ringworm. He had a flu-like illness at the time, which resolved. He worked as a tree surgeon in Michigan. He sustained insect bites regularly while working but did not recall a tick bite. Investigations: Borrelia burgdorferi IgG positive He was started on doxycycline 100 mg BD
questions.lead_in: What is the most appropriate advice about prognosis?

options.text: He is likely to have long-term sequelae
He should expect other joints to become involved despite completing treatment
His symptoms should resolve in 2–4 weeks of starting therapy
His symptoms should resolve in several months
His symptoms should resolve within 48 hours of starting treatment

questions.explanation: His symptoms should resolve in 2–4 weeks of starting therapy Ninety percent of patients show symptom resolution within 2–4 weeks of commencing therapy.
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 8 Q13

questions.stem: A 14-year-old boy presented to his primary care physician following a tick bite. The tick was unnoticed for 36 hours, and his mother was very concerned about him developing Lyme disease. Local tick infection rate with Borrelia is low. The boy had no relevant past medical history. Clinical examination was unremarkable.
questions.lead_in: What is the most appropriate action?

options.text: Request acute and convalescent serology for Lyme disease
Give doxycycline 100mg stat
Reassure but advise the family to be vigilant for erythema migrans
Start 14 days of amoxicillin 500 mg TDS
Perform a skin biopsy at the site of the tick bite

questions.explanation: Reassure but advise the family to be vigilant for erythema migrans There is no evidence of infection. Serology is not advised simply following a tick bite. Prophylaxis is not advised in this scenario when the local tick infection rate with Borrelia is low. Skin biopsy is not indicated.
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 9 Q14

questions.stem: A 59-year-old man was seen with a recurrence of fevers and chills. He was on day 7 of a 2-week course of doxycycline (100 mg BID) for presumed Lyme disease. He was a deer hunter from Nantucket, who had first presented with a 5-day history of a circular rash on his back, associated with fevers and chills. The rash had cleared, and his systemic symptoms had settled on starting doxycycline.
questions.lead_in: What is the most appropriate treatment?

options.text: Atovaquone and azithromycin PO for 7 days
Ceftriaxone IV followed by doxycycline PO to complete 21 days
Ceftriaxone IV for 21 days
Clindamycin and chloroquine PO for 7 days
Doxycycline PO for 21 days

questions.explanation: Atovaquone and azithromycin PO for 7 days The most likely explanation is a co-infection with babesiosis. Ixodes scapularis is the vector for Lyme disease, human anaplasmosis, and babesiosis. It is likely that he was appropriately diagnosed with early Lyme disease (given classic bull’s-eye skin rash). Although he initially responded, he had a deterioration which is classic for co-infection with babesiosis. Babesia has a slightly longer incubation period and tends to occur later. In contrast to anaplasmosis, Babesia is not covered by doxycycline. Chloroquine has no activity against Babesia either. The current recommended therapy is atovaquone and azithromycin for 7–10 days.
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 1 Q32

questions.question: Compare modified two-tier testing (MDTT) with standard two-tier testing (SDTT) for Lyme disease.
questions.question_raw: Lyme disease modified double tier testing vs standard double tier testing

parts.text: Explain how MDTT is different from SDTT.
Name two advantages and two disadvantages of MDTT.

parts_raw.text: Explain how MDTT is different from SDTT
Name 2 advantages and 2 disadvantages for MDTT

questions.model_answer: a) Standard two-tier testing = a first-tier sonicate EIA/ELISA, and equivocal or positive samples are then confirmed by IgM and IgG Western blot. Modified two-tier testing replaces the Western blot with a second EIA: a sonicate ELISA followed by an IgG VlsE C6-peptide enzyme immunoassay, so no immunoblot (and no IgM testing) is required. b) Advantages: (1) eliminates the subjective, labour-intensive Western blot and the need for IgM testing — the result is a straightforward seropositive/seronegative report; (2) better specificity than the C6 ELISA alone with comparable sensitivity, and it is especially useful to support the diagnosis of early Lyme disease. Disadvantages: (1) it loses the information a Western blot can give about duration of infection or reinfection, so the blot-based approach remains preferable for complex cases; (2) like the sonicate tests, the anti-VlsE response persists for months to years after successful treatment, so seropositivity cannot distinguish active from past infection.
questions.beyond_mandell: The CDC formally endorsed modified (EIA/EIA) two-tier testing in 2019.

questions.model_answer: a) In North America: Borrelia burgdorferi (the sole established cause in the US) and the newly recognized upper-midwestern species Borrelia mayonii. b) Ixodes scapularis (deer/blacklegged tick, Northeast and Midwest) and Ixodes pacificus (West). c) 6-yo, EM, anaphylaxis to penicillin: avoid amoxicillin and (given anaphylaxis) cephalosporins — use a macrolide, e.g. erythromycin 30 mg/kg/day divided (or azithromycin) x 14–21 days. d) 14-yo isolated Bell's (facial) palsy: oral regimen is adequate — doxycycline 100 mg PO BID (age ≥8) x 14–21 days. e) 28-yo Lyme meningitis, hospitalized: ceftriaxone 2 g IV once daily x 14–28 days (penicillin G or cefotaxime are alternatives). f) 6-yo Lyme arthritis: oral amoxicillin (age <8) 50 mg/kg/day divided, for ~28–30 days. g) 8-yo engorged tick, highly endemic area: single-dose doxycycline prophylaxis. h) 20-yo pregnant with EM: amoxicillin 500 mg PO TID x 14–21 days (doxycycline is contraindicated in pregnancy).
questions.beyond_mandell: Single-dose doxycycline 200 mg tick-bite prophylaxis (part g) is IDSA guidance, not in this chapter; current IDSA/AAP guidance also permits short (≤21-day) doxycycline courses in children <8.

questions.model_answer: a) 6-yo EM: amoxicillin (age <8) 50 mg/kg/day divided TID x 14–21 days (cefuroxime axetil or a macrolide if penicillin-allergic). b) 24-yo EM: doxycycline 100 mg PO BID x 14–21 days. c) 40-yo facial nerve palsy: oral regimen is adequate for isolated palsy — doxycycline 100 mg PO BID (up to TID) x 14–21 days. d) Arthritis: oral doxycycline 100 mg BID or amoxicillin 500 mg for 30 days (first-line); IV ceftriaxone 2 g daily x 14–28 days if no response. e) Meningitis: ceftriaxone 2 g IV ONCE DAILY x 14–28 days (penicillin G or cefotaxime are alternatives). f) The two most common vectors: Ixodes scapularis (Northeast/Midwest) and Ixodes pacificus (West).
questions.cohort_conflict: Mandell 9e Table 241.2 recommends amoxicillin (not doxycycline) for the 6-year-old; the cohort's use of the same doxycycline regimen in young children reflects newer CPS/IDSA guidance permitting short doxycycline courses.

cohort_answer.text: 6yo and 24yo EM: same treatment regimen (doxycycline can be used in peds if course is 2 weeks or less, per Canadian Pediatric Society and 2020 guidelines). Facial nerve palsy (40yo): no recommendation for or against steroids; note ceftriaxone dosing is DAILY for meningitis/CNS disease, not BID. Arthritis: duration 28 days, PO therapy suggested first-line, dosing same as EM. Meningitis: duration 14-21 days, CRO dosing daily; if hospitalized use CRO, if ambulatory use doxycycline (even pediatric) aiming for 14 day course; alternatives = PCN and cefotaxime. Two most common tick vectors: Ixodes scapularis (blacklegged/deer tick - northeastern, mid-Atlantic, north-central US); Ixodes pacificus (western blacklegged tick - Pacific Coast). Tick must be attached 36-48+ hours before transmission typically occurs.

questions.model_answer: a) STTT = a first-tier sonicate EIA/ELISA with confirmation of equivocal/positive samples by IgM and IgG Western blot. MTTT replaces the Western blot with a second enzyme immunoassay — a sonicate ELISA followed by an IgG VlsE C6-peptide EIA — so no immunoblot and no IgM testing are needed. b) Advantages: (1) eliminates the subjective Western blot and IgM testing, giving a straightforward seropositive/seronegative result; (2) better specificity than C6 ELISA alone with comparable sensitivity, particularly useful for early Lyme disease. Disadvantages: (1) loses the Western blot's information about duration of infection or reinfection, so the blot-based test remains preferable for complex cases; (2) the VlsE/C6 antibody response persists for months to years after treatment, so a positive result cannot distinguish active from past infection.

questions.question: Lyme disease serologic testing.
questions.question_raw: Lyme disease testing.

parts.text: What is modified two-tier testing compared to standard two-tier testing?
What are two advantages of modified two-tier testing, and two disadvantages (besides cost)?

parts_raw.text: What is modified two-tier testing compared to standard two-tier testing?
What are two advantages of MTTT, and two disadvantages (besides cost)?

questions.model_answer:
a) Standard two-tier testing is a first-tier whole-cell sonicate enzyme immunoassay (ELISA/EIA), and specimens that are equivocal or positive are confirmed by a second-tier IgM and IgG Western blot. Modified two-tier testing replaces the Western blot with a second EIA: a whole-cell sonicate EIA followed by an IgG VlsE C6 peptide EIA, so two sequential EIAs are used and IgM testing is eliminated.
b) Advantages: (1) It eliminates the need for IgM testing and Western blotting, and gives the clinician a straightforward seropositive/seronegative result. (2) It has nearly comparable sensitivity to the C6 peptide EIA alone with better specificity (comparable to conventional ELISA + Western blot), making it most valuable for supporting the diagnosis of early Lyme disease. Disadvantages (besides cost): (1) Unlike the Western blot, it cannot provide information on the duration of infection or whether reinfection has occurred, so it is less useful for complex cases. (2) The anti-VlsE antibody response (like sonicate responses) may persist for months to years after successful treatment, so a positive result cannot be equated with current or recent active infection.

questions.model_answer:
a) (1) Borrelia burgdorferi; (2) Borrelia mayonii (upper midwestern United States).
b) (1) Ixodes scapularis (northeastern/midwestern US); (2) Ixodes pacificus (western US).
c) (see individual scenarios d-h below for agent and duration).
d) 6-year-old, penicillin anaphylaxis, EM: child <8 years, so doxycycline/amoxicillin are not first choices; with penicillin anaphylaxis the cephalosporin cefuroxime is best avoided, so a macrolide (erythromycin 30 mg/kg/day, or azithromycin) for 14-21 days.
e) Pregnant woman, EM: amoxicillin 500 mg PO TID for 14-21 days (doxycycline avoided in pregnancy).
f) Man, isolated facial nerve palsy: oral regimen is adequate - doxycycline 100 mg PO BID for 14-21 days.
g) 44-year-old woman, Lyme meningitis (objective neurologic involvement): IV ceftriaxone 2 g once daily for 14-28 days (cefotaxime or penicillin G are alternatives).
h) 8-year-old, engorged tick removed in endemic area: if an engorged I. scapularis tick is identified, give a single 200 mg dose of doxycycline within 72 hours of removal; otherwise observe and treat only if signs of Lyme disease develop.
questions.beyond_mandell: For the penicillin-anaphylaxis child, the IDSA short-course doxycycline option (any age) is an alternative to the macrolide listed in Mandell's table.

questions.model_answer:
a) (1) Ixodes scapularis; (2) Ixodes pacificus.
b) Other agents transmitted by I. scapularis: (1) Babesia microti (babesiosis); (2) Anaplasma phagocytophilum (anaplasmosis); (3) Borrelia miyamotoi (and Borrelia mayonii); (4) Powassan (deer tick) encephalitis virus.
c) IDSA criteria (all must be met): (1) the attached tick is identified as an I. scapularis (or I. pacificus) nymph or adult and estimated to have been attached >=36 hours (engorgement/exposure history); (2) prophylaxis can be started within 72 hours of tick removal; (3) the local rate of tick infection with B. burgdorferi is high (highly endemic area, >=20%); (4) doxycycline is not contraindicated. When met, give a single 200 mg dose of doxycycline.
questions.beyond_mandell: The four specific prophylaxis criteria (36 h attachment, 72 h window, >=20% local infection rate, no contraindication) are from the IDSA Lyme disease guidelines; Mandell states only the engorged I. scapularis + single 200 mg doxycycline within 72 h rule.

parts.text: What is the difference between the modified test and the standard two-tier test?
Give two advantages and two disadvantages of the modified two-tier test (2 x 2 table format).

parts_raw.text: What is the difference between the modified test and standard two tier test?
2 advantages and 2 disadvantages of the modified two tier test (2 x 2 table format)

questions.model_answer:
a) Standard two-tier: a whole-cell sonicate EIA/ELISA first, with equivocal or positive samples confirmed by IgM and IgG Western blot. Modified two-tier: two sequential EIAs - a whole-cell sonicate EIA followed by an IgG VlsE C6 peptide EIA - with no Western blot and no IgM testing.
b)
| Advantages | Disadvantages |
| (1) Eliminates IgM testing and Western blot; gives a simple seropositive/seronegative result. | (1) Cannot indicate duration of infection or reinfection (unlike the Western blot), so less useful in complex cases. |
| (2) Comparable sensitivity to C6 EIA with better specificity (similar to ELISA + blot); best for supporting diagnosis of early Lyme disease. | (2) Anti-VlsE response persists for months-years after treatment, so a positive result cannot confirm current/recent active infection. |

cohort_answer.text: Standard: EIA (high sensitivity) followed by confirmatory Western Blot (higher specificity); Modified: two EIAs with different targets. Advantages (MTT): better sensitivity for early disease without compromising specificity, cheaper, faster TAT, less labor intensive. Disadvantages (MTT): lower sensitivity for late disease (vs standard), can't distinguish recent from past infection.

questions.model_answer:
a) Borrelia burgdorferi and Borrelia mayonii.
b) Ixodes scapularis and Ixodes pacificus.
c) EM, 8-year-old: doxycycline 100 mg PO BID for 14-21 days (recommended from age 8; a 10-day course is equivalent), with amoxicillin as the alternative in younger/pregnant patients.
d) EM, adult: doxycycline 100 mg PO BID for 14-21 days (amoxicillin or cefuroxime axetil are alternatives).
e) Arthritis, 10-year-old: oral doxycycline or amoxicillin for 30 days (30-60 days); IV ceftriaxone for 14-28 days if poor response.
f) Isolated CN (facial) palsy, adult: oral regimen is adequate - doxycycline 100 mg PO BID/TID for 14-21 days.
g) Meningitis, adult: IV ceftriaxone 2 g once daily for 14-28 days (objective neurologic involvement warrants parenteral therapy; penicillin G or cefotaxime are alternatives).
h) Child with engorged tick removed: if an engorged I. scapularis is identified in an endemic area, give a single 200 mg dose of doxycycline within 72 hours; otherwise observe and treat only if Lyme disease develops.
questions.cohort_conflict: For meningitis the cohort answer gives oral doxycycline, but Mandell recommends IV ceftriaxone for objective neurologic involvement such as meningitis (oral regimens are reserved for facial palsy alone).

cohort_answer.text: a) Borrelia burgdorferi and Borrelia mayonii. b) Ixodes scapularis and Ixodes pacificus. c) Doxycycline for 10 days. d) Doxycycline for 10 days. e) Doxycycline for 28 days. f) Doxycycline for 14-21 days. g) Doxycycline x14-21 days. h) Prophylaxis single dose doxycycline if meets ALL criteria: attached tick identified as Ixodes scapularis/pacificus; tick estimated attached >36h; prophylaxis begun within 72h of tick removal; bite in highly endemic area; doxycycline not contraindicated. If criteria not met, observe and treat only if signs/symptoms of Lyme disease (EM) develop.

questions.model_answer:
a) (1) Ixodes scapularis (deer tick) — vector in the northeastern and midwestern US; (2) Ixodes pacificus — vector in the western US.
b) (1) Babesia microti; (2) Anaplasma phagocytophilum; (3) Borrelia miyamotoi; (4) Powassan (deer tick) encephalitis virus. (Borrelia mayonii and Ehrlichia sp. Wisconsin are also accepted.)
c) (1) Tick identified as an adult or nymphal Ixodes scapularis; (2) tick attached >=36 hours (engorged); (3) prophylaxis begun within 72 hours of tick removal; (4) bite in a highly endemic area, with no contraindication to doxycycline. Regimen: single 200 mg dose of doxycycline.
questions.beyond_mandell: Mandell states prophylaxis with a single 200 mg doxycycline dose for an engorged nymphal I. scapularis within 72 h (p. 2921); the discrete >=36 h attachment and high-endemicity thresholds are from the IDSA Lyme guideline (Wormser et al.).

cohort_answer.text: Tick species: Ixodes scapularis; Ixodes pacificus. Other pathogens: Babesia microti; Borrelia miyamotoi; Borrelia mayonii; Anaplasma phagocytophilum; Powassan virus. IDSA prophylaxis criteria: Tick identified as an adult or nymphal Ixodes species; Attached >=36 hours; Prophylaxis begun within 72 hours of tick removal; Bite occurs in a highly endemic area; No contraindication to doxy. Second line agents for treatment (not proph) include amoxicillin or cefuroxime 14 days; if unable to use doxy or beta-lactam, azithromycin for 7 days is third line

questions.model_answer: a) Babesia microti (the Maltese-cross tetrad is pathognomonic of small Babesia spp.; on the eastern seaboard the agent is B. microti). b) Ixodes scapularis (nymph is the primary vector). c) Four of: (1) asplenia (2) malignancy (3) HIV/AIDS with low CD4 count (4) TNF-alpha blockade / immunosuppression for transplant or B-cell lymphoma (also X-linked agammaglobulinemia, rituximab). d) Oral atovaquone 750 mg q12h plus IV azithromycin 500 mg/day for 7-10 days (first-line); alternative clindamycin 600 mg q6h IV plus quinine 650 mg q6-8h PO. Consider RBC exchange transfusion if parasitemia >=10%, Hgb <10 g/dL, or organ compromise. e) Borrelia burgdorferi (Lyme) and Anaplasma phagocytophilum.
questions.cohort_conflict: Mandell 9e lists atovaquone plus IV azithromycin as first-line for severe B. microti disease, with clindamycin plus quinine as the alternative, whereas the cohort answer names clindamycin plus quinine as the treatment for severe disease.

cohort_answer.text: Organism: Babesia microti (can look like P. falciparum on smear). Vector: Ixodes scapularis. Risk factors for severe babesia: Asplenia, >50 yo, malignancy, immunocompromised state, HIV/AIDS, liver disease, TNF inhibitors. Treatment for severe babesia: Quinine + clindamycin (atovaquone + azithro for mild-mod). Other organisms same vector: Borrelia burgdorferi, Anaplasma phagocytophilum, Borrelia mayonii, Ehrlichia
